notes.meaning: God answers Moses' distress by assuring him that Pharaoh will not only release the Israelites, but will actively drive them away. Human power had completely failed, making this the right moment for God to step in and show His strength. Pharaoh's hard heart will bend only when God's mighty power forces him to yield.

God introduces His message by stating His personal name, the LORD (Yahweh). This name presents God as the unchanging, eternal One who always keeps His promises. By speaking His name, God reminds Moses that the Almighty Himself is backing this mission.

Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob knew God as 'God Almighty,' experiencing His great power to protect and bless their families. While they had heard the name Yahweh, they had not yet seen the full meaning of that name displayed through the actual fulfillment of the covenant promises. Now God is about to make that name real to Israel by rescuing the whole nation.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars argue that this verse reflects an ancient written source that believed the name Yahweh was unknown until the time of Moses.

notes.meaning: God reminds Moses of the covenant He made with the patriarchs to give them Canaan as their homeland. A covenant is a sacred, unbreakable promise made by God. Even though Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob lived there only as wandering foreigners, God's pledge to give them the land remained entirely firm.

God declares that He has heard the desperate cries of the enslaved Israelites and has remembered His covenant. In the Bible, God 'remembering' does not mean He had forgotten, but that the appointed time has arrived for Him to take action. The worsening cruelty of Egypt only moved God to step forward in mercy.

Moses is sent to give Israel three clear promises of freedom: God will lift their heavy burdens, rescue them from slavery, and redeem them with mighty power. To redeem means to buy back a family member from bondage and set them free. God will bare His arm in judgment against Egypt to deliver His people.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Many teachers link the four promises of rescue in verses 6 and 7 to the four cups of wine used in the traditional Jewish Passover meal.

notes.meaning: God promises to adopt Israel as His own special nation and to be their God. Through this miraculous deliverance from slavery, the Israelites will come to know firsthand that the Lord is their true protector. God rescues His people so they can live in a close, lasting relationship with Him.

God promises to lead the Israelites into the land He swore to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, giving it to them as an enduring possession. The phrase 'I swore' reflects God lifting His hand to take a solemn oath. The promise closes with 'I am the LORD,' stamping the pledge with His supreme authority.

Moses shared all of these encouraging promises with the Israelites, but they were too worn down to listen. Constant slave labor and bitter disappointment had broken their spirits. When grief and pain become intense, it can be very difficult for people to take in the comfort of God's word.

Even though Israel rejected the message, the Lord spoke to Moses once again. He commanded him to go directly to Pharaoh and order him to let the Israelites leave Egypt. God graciously repeats His instructions before He begins pouring out His judgments on a rebellious ruler.

Moses objected before the Lord, arguing that if his own people would not listen, a proud foreign king certainly never would. He also pleaded that he was 'unskilled in speech,' literally having 'uncircumcised lips.' In Hebrew thinking, something uncircumcised was closed off or unfit for its work, expressing Moses' deep feeling of inadequacy.

Rather than debating Moses' objections, the Lord placed a solemn, royal charge on both Moses and Aaron. He commanded them to address both Israel and Pharaoh and to bring the people out of Egypt. God's supreme authority settles all excuses and calls His servants to obey without arguing.

The story pauses to provide a family record that establishes the lineage of Moses and Aaron among the tribes of Israel. It begins by listing the clan leaders of Reuben, Jacob's firstborn son, followed by the sons of Simeon. These older brothers are named first so the family tree can move in orderly fashion toward Levi.

Levi was the third son of Jacob, and his sons Gershon, Kohath, and Merari became the founders of the priestly tribe. Levi lived to be 137 years old. Recording his age and family branches roots the coming deliverance in true Israelite history.

These verses name the sons of Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, identifying the major clans of the tribe of Levi. Kohath lived 133 years and is singled out because he was the direct ancestor of Moses and Aaron. Although Kohath was not the eldest son, God sovereignly chose his family line for the priesthood.

Amram married Jochebed, and she gave birth to Aaron and Moses; Amram lived to the age of 137 years. Moses wrote down this marriage honestly even though later biblical law would forbid marrying an aunt. He cared more about recording the plain truth than protecting his own family's reputation.

differ.view: Some Baptists take the text literally to mean Amram married his biological aunt, which was permissible before the law in Leviticus later banned it.
Some Methodists interpret the Hebrew term as a near relative or cousin rather than an aunt.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that several generations are omitted between Kohath and Moses, since the Kohathite clan already numbered thousands by the time of the Exodus.

notes.meaning: These verses list the sons of Izhar and Uzziel, who were uncles to Moses and Aaron. Among them was Korah, who would later lead a well-known rebellion against Moses in the wilderness. The biblical record includes him faithfully without attempting to hide family trouble.

Aaron married Elisheba, the sister of Nahshon, a high-ranking prince from the royal tribe of Judah. She gave birth to four sons: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. This marriage tied the priestly family to the tribe of Judah and established the line of Israel's future priests.

The list records the sons of Korah as well as Eleazar's son Phinehas, who would later stand boldly for God's honor. These names preserved the record of the leading priestly and Levite families for future generations. Moses carefully detailed Aaron's family tree because the high priesthood belonged to his household.

The genealogy concludes by pointing out that these were the very same men, Aaron and Moses, whom God ordered to lead Israel out like an organized army. They were the ones who stood in Pharaoh's court to speak on behalf of the people. While Aaron is listed first by birth order, Moses stands out as God's chosen deliverer.

The narrative returns to the exact moment God gave His command in Egypt before the genealogy was inserted. The Lord reiterated His supreme name, 'I am the LORD,' reminding Moses of who held the authority. He then ordered Moses to speak every word God gave him directly to Pharaoh.

Moses repeated his complaint that his speech was awkward and clumsy, questioning why Pharaoh would ever listen to him. Since his own people had already turned away, he felt completely inadequate for such a difficult task. Moses' natural weakness makes it clear that the coming victory belonged entirely to God.
